requested.title: Clearance token has no binding to the client that solved the proof-of-work, so one solve is infinitely shareable
Interstitial mints a captcha and runs a full SSR render on every blocked request, upstream of every rate limiter
`handle` middleware, `transformPage`, and `filterResponseHeaders` never run for the interstitial, so app security headers are silently absent from it
`protect` JSDoc states publicDir files are never gated, contradicting the default `protectFiles: true`
Unauthenticated page mints 4 captcha capability tokens per request with no rate limit, bypassing the 60/min cap on the site's dedicated mint endpoint
`defaultsSample` omits three of the component's CSS custom properties, on the page that documents them

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified end-to-end. `mintClearanceToken(bits)` seals exactly `JSON.stringify({ iat: Date.now(), bits })` under `PROTECTION_AAD` (clearance.ts:13) — no IP, no UA, no `jti`, no server-side issuance record. `hasValidClearance(cookieValue, maxAgeMs, minBits)` takes no request or context argument at all (clearance.ts:20), so binding is architecturally impossible, not merely omitted; it checks only the AES-SIV seal, `typeof iat === 'number'`, `bits >= minBits`, and `-30_000 <= ageMs < maxAgeMs`. The gate's only check is `hasValidClearance(input.cookies.get(options.cookieName), options.maxAgeMs, options.bits)` (gate.ts:152). I read every file in `packages/mochi/src/protection/` (clearance, config, gate, types) plus `protection.test.ts` and found no fingerprinting anywhere: the test suite covers seal tampering, expiry, clock skew, bits floor, and AAD cross-spending (a captcha token is refused as a clearance) — and nothing about the requester, confirming this is the intended design. The cookie attributes (`httpOnly`, `sameSite: 'lax'`, `secure`) at Mochi.ts:1789-1795 stop XSS theft and some CSRF but are irrelevant to voluntary sharing; the attacker is the solver, who reads `Set-Cookie` off their own verify response — exactly what `protectionServe.test.ts` does (it lifts the clearance cookie via `clearanceCookieFrom(verified.setCookie!)` and replays it on later `fetch` calls, including against `publicDir` files). Concrete attack: solve once at 19-20 bits (~1s of CPU), POST to `/_mochi/protection/verify`, extract the cookie, hand it to N distributed scrapers for the full 4-hour `maxAgeMs`. Protection mode's entire value is imposing per-client proof-of-work cost; unbounded transferability amortizes that to ~0, and with no server-side record there is no revocation and no way to notice one token arriving from thousands of addresses. The peer comparison is apt — Anubis derives its challenge from the client IP/UA/Accept-Language, and Cloudflare's `cf_clearance` binds similarly — while `152-protection.md` markets this as 'Cloudflare-style browser verification' and discloses only that the clearance is 'a sealed `{ iat }` token ... keyed off MOCHI_KEY'. Keeping MEDIUM: this is a real, concrete defeat of the control's cost model in every deployment that enables it. I note the finding's `auth-bypass` slug is a misnomer — protection mode is not authentication (anyone may solve and enter), so the impact is anti-abuse efficacy, not access control; and the marginal benefit of binding is bounded, since a motivated adversary can pay one sub-second solve per IP anyway. That bounds severity at MEDIUM but does not make the gap unreal.

Every ordering fact checks out, but the security thesis does not. Confirmed: `blockedResponse` routes page/fallback GET|HEAD to `interstitialResponse` (gate.ts:129-131), which calls `mintCaptcha()` (L86) and does a fresh `registry.renderComponent` + `renderShell` per request (L102-111) with no memoization; the gate holds no limiter (grep for `rateLimit|limiter` in `protection/` returns nothing); and the gate runs inside `buildRequestContext` (requestSetup.ts:130-136) whose `earlyResponse` returns at Mochi.ts:971-973, i.e. before `checkRouteLimit` (L981) and before `middleware` (L991) — same shape for api (L1201 vs L1211). The verify endpoint is indeed a bare `bunRoutes` entry (L1812-1813). What fails is the claim that 'the cheapest request forces one of the most expensive operations on the request path.' I read `ProtectionShell.svelte` (a single `<div>`/`<main>`/logo/one `MochiCaptchaAuto` island), `renderComponent` (ComponentRegistry.ts:1640-1798) and `createShellRenderer`. The component is pre-compiled at boot (it is pushed into `ssrEntrypoints` at Mochi.ts:680-682), so the `await this.compile()` at L1645 is a Map-hit no-op (`compileAll` early-returns when `todo.length === 0`, L728-730); the remaining work is a Svelte SSR render of a ~3KB tree, three regexes plus one `replaceAll`, one HTMLRewriter pass, and string substitution into a precomputed shell. That is strictly *less* work than the real page it displaces, which runs the identical machinery over a larger tree *plus* the app's `serverProps` (DB/network). So enabling protection lowers, not raises, the per-request cost of an uncleared GET flood — the inversion claim is backwards. Crucially there is also no state to exhaust: `mintCaptcha` only `randomUUID()`s and AES-SIV-seals (captcha.ts:43-52); nothing touches the nonce store until `verifyCaptcha` consumes, which requires a genuinely solved token. And every other kind — api, ws, sse, file, and all non-GET — short-circuits to a static `Response.json`/text 403 with no render at all (gate.ts:132-135), which covers most hostile traffic. Two further corrections: for `fallback` kind the gate runs *inside* the middleware chain (`composedFetch` L1898-1903 sits within `innerResolve`, invoked by `middleware({event, resolve})` at L1922), so a middleware limiter *does* apply there — 'never' is wrong; and Mochi's page cache is opt-in app-level, so the only scenario where the interstitial is the slower path requires the operator to have explicitly cached that route. Memoizing the interstitial with a token placeholder is a fair performance nit (the finding's own recommendation), but 'a dynamic endpoint costs sub-millisecond CPU and has no attachable limiter' is not a bypassed control or an exploitable amplification.

Confirmed for the dominant case. The interstitial is built with only `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control: no-store` (gate.ts:119-122) and returned through `finalizeCookieHeaders` (L155); because the gate lives in `buildRequestContext` (requestSetup.ts:130-136) that response exits as `earlyResponse` and the page handler returns it at Mochi.ts:971-973, several lines before `middleware` runs at L991. I traced `transformPage`/`filterResponseHeaders` to `applyResolveOptions` in `runtime/hooks.ts:162-190`, driven only by a `resolve(event, opts)` call from inside a `Handle` — so both are middleware-scoped and both are skipped along with the chain. I independently verified the premise that makes this matter: a case-insensitive grep across all of `packages/mochi/src` for `content-security-policy`, `x-frame-options`, and `strict-transport-security` returns nothing, and `packages/docs/120-middleware.md:98-115` documents `resolve(event, opts)`/middleware as the place to shape response headers. This repo's own `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts` is exactly that pattern — a `Handle` that awaits `resolve(event)` then rebuilds the Response to `set('Content-Security-Policy', ...)`, with an in-file comment noting `filterResponseHeaders` 'can only drop headers, never add one' — mounted at `support/src/index.ts:41` via `sequence(adminAuth, embedHeaders, analytics(...))`. An app on that pattern that enables `protection` would ship its one JS-executing, every-first-time-visitor page with no CSP while every other page is covered. Two refinements, neither fatal: (a) for `fallback` kind the gate runs *inside* `composedFetch`'s middleware chain (Mochi.ts:1898-1903, wrapped by L1922) and the blocked response goes through `applyResolveOptions`, so fallback interstitials *do* get middleware — the finding's unqualified 'never' is too strong, though page routes are the primary and intended protection target; (b) error pages are unaffected because `routeErrorResponse` is invoked inside `inner`, making the interstitial genuinely anomalous among the framework's HTML responses. The finding's own scoping is honest and matches my reading: all five interstitial props are server-generated and Svelte-escaped, so this is lost defense-in-depth with no injection vector. BUG is the right severity; the claim is accurate.

Straightforwardly correct, and the file contradicts itself. The `protect` JSDoc at types.ts:13-17 reads 'Framework client assets, `publicDir` files, warmup self-requests, the verify endpoint, and unmatched 404s are never gated' — yet 14 lines later in the *same interface*, the `protectFiles` doc comment at types.ts:31 says 'Gate `publicDir` static files too (subject to `protect()`). Default: `true`.' I verified all three corroborating sources the finding cites: `config.ts:43` resolves `protectFiles: opts.protectFiles ?? true`; `Mochi.ts:1845-1859` builds `publicRouteGuard` whenever `protectionRuntime && protectionRuntime.options.protectFiles` and runs `protectionRuntime.gate({ ..., kind: 'file' })` before `serve()`, passing it to `registerPublicRoutes`; and `packages/docs/152-protection.md:51` states the opposite in bold — 'publicDir static files **are** gated (as kind `file`) — set `protectFiles: false` to leave them open'. The test coverage confirms the runtime behaviour: `protectionServe.test.ts` has 'publicDir static files are gated by default (protectFiles) and open with clearance', asserting 403 for `/hello.txt` with no cookie and 200 (plus `Vary: Cookie`) with clearance. The secondary claim also holds: docs L51 lists 'the image and local-asset endpoints' among the never-gated surfaces and the JSDoc omits them. Since this JSDoc is the editor tooltip a developer reads while writing `protect()`, the realistic consequence is an operator believing static assets stay publicly reachable when they are in fact behind the gate, or not discovering `protectFiles: false`. No exploit path — it is a documentation defect with deployment-availability consequences, so BUG is correct.

All of the finding's factual premises verify, but no control is bypassed and the attacker gains nothing. Confirmed: `serverProps: () => ({ captchas: [mintCaptcha(), mintCaptcha(), mintCaptcha(), mintCaptcha()] })` with no `rateLimit`; `captchaStylingRoutes` spread unconditionally at `site/routes.ts:354` (well outside the `DEVELOPMENT` block at L275-280); no global `rateLimit` in `site/index.ts`; `checkRouteLimit` no-ops without a limiter (Mochi.ts:862-864); tokens seal only `{iat, nonce, bits}` under the constant `CAPTCHA_AAD` (captcha.ts:50) at the default 19 bits. But the 60/min on `/api/captcha-demo/mint` is endpoint hygiene on a bare JSON route (its comment says it exists so `/blog/:slug` 'stays post-agnostic'), not a boundary metering token supply — and token supply is not a security-relevant scarce resource here. Minting allocates zero server state (no nonce-store write until `verifyCaptcha` consumes), and it does not reduce the actual control, which is the per-token ~2^19-hash proof-of-work the attacker must still pay for every submission. Uncapped minting is in fact the normal shape across this repo: `/demos/captcha` on site mints per GET uncapped, support's `/` form mints per GET with no `rateLimit` on the route at all, and the newsletter embed mints per GET with its limiter *deliberately* `skip`ped for non-POST (`skip: (req) => req.method !== 'POST'`). That last one is decisive evidence the author does not treat mint-rate as a control surface. The pre-aging angle adds nothing either: an attacker can always satisfy `minAgeMs = 2000` by fetching the target's own form page and waiting two seconds, so harvesting remotely is not a bypass of the timing floor. There is no bits downgrade — 19 bits matches every other mint site on the site, and the one security-relevant consumer, protection mode, verifies with `minBits: protectionOptions.bits` where `site/index.ts:193` sets `bits: 20`, so these tokens are refused for clearance (the finding concedes this). The cross-deployment escalation requires a shared `MOCHI_KEY` across two separately-deployed apps, which is assumed rather than shown; and even granting it, support's mail-sending `/` form has no rate limit *and* mints its own tokens unmetered, so harvested tokens buy no capability, while the newsletter's side-effecting POST is capped at 20/10m with `ban: { threshold: 3, duration: '1h' }` — throughput there is bounded by the POST limiter regardless of token inventory. Finally, this is `packages/site/src/demos/*`, which the project context designates demonstration code to be judged as documentation. Adding a `rateLimit` and not minting four unused tokens on a pure styling page is a reasonable hardening nit, but there is no exploitable bypass.

Verified by direct enumeration. `grep -n 'var(--mochi-captcha' packages/mochi/src/captcha/MochiCaptcha.svelte` yields 15 usages across exactly 12 distinct custom properties. `defaultsSample` (themes.ts:53-64) lists 9, and all 9 match the component's fallbacks precisely: `hint-text` #6e756d (L392/448), `border` #e8e4d8 (L398), `radius` 999px (L399/408/419), `track-bg` #faf8f1 (L400), `accent-soft` #e0ebe1 (L407), `handle-bg` #fffdf8 (L420), `accent` #4a7c59 (L421), `handle-text` → `var(--mochi-captcha-accent, #4a7c59)` (L422), `accent-soft-text` #2f5b3f (L453). The three error-state vars are absent exactly as described: `--mochi-captcha-error-bg` (#fdf3f2, L468), `--mochi-captcha-error-border` (#e9c9c4, L469), `--mochi-captcha-error-text` (#8a3324, L487). So the sample's own comment, 'Each var's built-in fallback', is false, and this is precisely the drift the file header sets out to prevent ('what the page shows can't drift from what it does') — that guarantee holds for the three `themes` entries, which feed both the live widgets and the rendered samples from one object, but `defaultsSample` is an unlinked duplicated literal. The practical consequence the finding describes is real and I can see it in the codebase: the framework's own `ProtectionShell.svelte` dark-mode block overrides all three `--mochi-captcha-error-*` vars, demonstrating that a serious themer does need them, while a reader working from this page would theme only the normal state and leave the error box at the stock off-white/red — visibly mismatched under the `terminal` theme, which sets `--mochi-captcha-radius: 0`. No security impact: the values are static, non-secret presentation defaults. BUG is the correct severity; the finding's own 'Confidence: medium' understates it — the claim is fully verifiable.
